cards.title: Optimal one-pass randomized space for LIS length
cards.formal:
Determine, up to constant factors, the optimal randomized one-pass streaming space in bits for a factor-two estimate of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of a length-\(n\) sequence over \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).

For every fixed input \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{1,\ldots,n\}^n\), let
\[L(x)=\max\{r:\exists\,1\le i_1<\cdots<i_r\le n,\ x_{i_1}<\cdots<x_{i_r}\}.\]
An admissible algorithm reads \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) once in this order and, after the final item, outputs an integer \(\widehat L\) such that
\[\Pr\bigl[L(x)/2\le\widehat L\le L(x)\bigr]\ge2/3.\]
Find an explicit asymptotic function \(f(n)\) admitting a uniform algorithm with \(O(f(n))\) worst-case bit space and a matching \(\Omega(f(n))\) lower bound for every admissible randomized algorithm. Logarithmic factors are part of the requested answer.
cards.why: This problem tests whether randomness can substantially reduce the memory needed to retain ordered structure in a sequence. The large gap between what is known for deterministic algorithms and what is proved necessary for ordinary randomized algorithms makes it a basic unresolved question about one-pass computation.
cards.status_note: Source-open in Sublinear.info Problem 44, Bertinoro 2011, updated 7 March 2013. The selected version uses one pass over length-n sequences from {1,...,n}, a factor-two underestimate and success at least 2/3. On 16 September 2026 the review checked the SODA 2007 upper bound, Chakrabarti’s 2010/2012 communication result and the published ITCS 2026 paper, whose introduction explicitly leaves ordinary randomized LIS approximation open. Its Theorem 1 is a white-box adversarial result for factor 1.1 and alphabet size at least 3n, so it does not resolve the selected model. A bounded later-work search found no verified matching randomized bounds; this does not certify the entire literature or supply a Lean proof.

progress.text: A deterministic one-pass approximation uses \(O(\sqrt n\log(n+2))\) bits for the selected alphabet and fixed accuracy, giving a valid randomized upper bound.

Chakrabarti proves that the communication problems behind earlier deterministic lower bounds have efficient randomized protocols. Those reductions therefore do not yield matching randomized lower bounds.

Gal, Kol, Saxena and Yu prove a square-root white-box lower bound with the additional model and accuracy conditions stated above; they still describe ordinary randomized LIS approximation as a longstanding open problem.

sentences: The problem asks for optimal bit space to estimate the longest strictly increasing subsequence in one streaming pass.
Inputs are arbitrary length-n sequences of numbers from one to n, fixed before the algorithm chooses its random bits.
The final estimate must lie between half the true length and the true length with probability at least two thirds.
Deterministic upper bounds and recent lower bounds against a stronger adaptive adversary leave the ordinary randomized optimum unresolved.
The requested answer must match upper and lower bounds up to constants, including every logarithmic factor.

cards.definitions:
The stream length \(n\ge1\) is known before the stream begins. The input contains exactly \(n\) integers, each in the ordered alphabet \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), represented in binary. Repetitions are allowed: the input is an arbitrary sequence and need not be a permutation. The asymptotic parameter is the number of items \(n\), whereas memory is measured in bits, not in stored items or machine words. An explicit input list occupies \(O(n\log(n+2))\) bits.

An increasing subsequence retains selected positions in their original order; the positions need not be consecutive. Both inequalities in its definition are strict. In particular, repeated equal values cannot both appear in such a subsequence. The strictly decreasing sequence has LIS length one, while \((1,2,\ldots,n)\) has LIS length \(n\). The problem asks only for the length estimate. It does not require the positions or values of a witnessing subsequence.

A single pass gives sequential access to the items from first to last, with no rewind, rereading, permutation of the stream or random-access queries to earlier positions. The algorithm may retain information about previous items only in its working memory. Its output appears after the whole sequence has been processed. It need not approximate the LIS of every prefix or issue intermediate answers.

For each fixed valid sequence, the probability is taken over independent fair random bits used by the algorithm. The entire input is fixed independently of those bits. The guarantee is required separately for every sequence, including sequences with short LIS; there is no promise that the LIS contains a constant fraction of the input. The algorithm may fail on at most one third of its random executions for a particular sequence. No distribution on input sequences is imposed.

The output convention is an underestimate within a factor two, as in the later paper's multiplicative approximation definition. On successful executions it lies in \([L(x)/2,L(x)]\). This is not the wider interval \([L(x)/2,2L(x)]\). The output can be an integer: rounding up a real output in the chosen interval preserves both bounds because \(L(x)\) is an integer. No additive error is allowed.

Use one finite uniform streaming program at all lengths. Its persistent state and temporary working storage are measured in bits; stored input values, counters, indices, retained random choices and output preparation all count. There is no external scratch storage, reusable random tape containing uncharged information, advice string or oracle. The stream itself is read-only sequential input. Fresh random bits may be consumed during computation; information about past bits can be reused only if it was retained within the counted memory.

Space is the maximum number of working bits used at any time, over every valid input of length \(n\) and every random execution, including executions whose final answer is inaccurate. Call this quantity \(s_A(n)\) for algorithm \(A\). It is not expected space. The algorithm must terminate after processing its input, but the target imposes no separate update-time or total-time bound. Unlimited local computation does not permit additional storage or another pass. Knowing \(n\) does not provide the input's LIS length or any statistic of the sequence.

The requested optimum means matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds in this model. There must be one admissible algorithm \(A_*\), a constant \(C>0\) and a threshold \(n_0\) with \(s_{A_*}(n)\le C f(n)\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). For every admissible randomized algorithm \(A\), there must be constants \(c_A>0,n_A\) with \(s_A(n)\ge c_A f(n)\) for all \(n\ge n_A\). The constants are independent of the input and its random bits. The answer must state \(f\) explicitly and establish both directions; merely defining \(f\) to be the unknown optimum is not an answer.

All factors growing with \(n\), including \(\log n\), iterated logarithms or a slowly growing multiplier, must be retained. Determining only an exponent in \(n\), or proving bounds that match only after hiding logarithmic factors, does not meet the selected precision. No numerical additive tolerance applies to an asymptotic space bound.

The white-box adversarial model is different: its input generator may inspect the algorithm's previous random choices and internal memory before selecting the next item. A lower bound against algorithms required to survive that stronger input generator need not hold when the sequence is fixed beforehand. Deterministic algorithms, multiple-pass algorithms, algorithms with reordered access and additive approximations are also separately specified variants. The original source mentions both one and constantly many passes; the user selected exactly one pass and the alphabet \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give an explicit function \(f(n)\) and complete Lean-checked proofs of the matching uniform upper and randomized lower space bounds defined above. The algorithm must meet the factor-two interval and success probability on every fixed input, using one pass and counted worst-case bit space. The lower bound must apply to randomized algorithms in this same fixed-input model and alphabet, not only to deterministic or white-box adversarial algorithms. A single improved bound without a matching other direction, an additive approximation, an algorithm for a larger approximation factor or bounds differing by a logarithmic factor do not complete the selected constant-factor determination.

context_blocks.text: The length of the longest increasing subsequence measures how much ordered structure survives inside a sequence. Computing or estimating it differs from sorting: only a number is requested, yet information from distant positions can determine which choices combine into a long subsequence.

Gopalan and coauthors give a deterministic one-pass approximation algorithm using \(O(\sqrt n)\) stored input symbols for fixed relative accuracy. With alphabet \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the corresponding bit bound is \(O(\sqrt n\log(n+2))\). Their discussion explains how to handle strict rather than nondecreasing subsequences. This is an upper bound for randomized algorithms as well, because they may ignore randomness.

Deterministic lower bounds leave open whether randomness saves substantially more memory. Chakrabarti shows that the communication problems used in those lower bounds admit inexpensive randomized protocols. This establishes a limitation of those particular lower-bound arguments; it does not provide a small-space randomized LIS algorithm.

The ITCS 2026 paper proves a square-root space lower bound in the white-box model for a 1.1-approximation with an alphabet of size at least three times the stream length. Its theorem differs from this card in the adversary, accuracy and stated alphabet. Its introduction explicitly retains the ordinary randomized approximation problem as open.

An additive approximation to LIS length can be useful when \(L(x)\) is large. An additive error proportional to \(n\), however, can exceed the entire answer when \(L(x)\ll n\). Likewise, an approximation to the complementary quantity \(n-L(x)\), the number of deletions needed to leave a strictly increasing sequence, need not approximate a small \(L(x)\) multiplicatively.

This is an unusual streaming question in which a sublinear-space deterministic algorithm is known but the benefit of randomness remains poorly understood. Matching randomized bounds would explain whether the memory cost comes from the ordered structure of the input or from limitations of deterministic summaries.

cards.title: Sublogarithmic distributed MIS
cards.formal:
In the randomized LOCAL model, does there exist an algorithm that finds a maximal independent set in $o(\log n)$ rounds on every $n$-vertex simple graph? Its output $I\subseteq V$ must satisfy $(u,v)\in E\Rightarrow\{u,v\}
subseteq I$ and $v
otin I\Rightarrow N(v)\cap I
e\varnothing$. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each fixed constant $c>0$, allowing the constant in the running time to depend on $c$. The bound must hold uniformly over all maximum degrees $\Delta\le n-1$.
cards.why: This isolates the communication needed for a basic symmetry-breaking task whose feasibility is easy to check locally. I include it because either outcome would change the benchmark for distributed graph algorithms: a faster algorithm would supply a stronger primitive, while a logarithmic lower bound would expose a substantial limitation of local coordination.
cards.definitions:
The network is the input graph. Rounds are synchronous; each edge can carry an arbitrarily large message in each direction. Vertices may have distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifiers and private random bits. Every vertex outputs its own membership bit. The measured time is the number of elapsed rounds until all outputs are available, not the number of rounds in which an individual processor stays awake.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree. Both the algorithm and the asymptotic time bound are uniform over input graphs and valid identifier assignments.

progress.text: Ghaffari gives the degree-sensitive MIS algorithm. With subsequent deterministic finishing routines, the standard bound is $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$.

Khoury and Schild give a randomized lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\log\Delta,\sqrt{\log n}\})$ for maximal matching and, by reduction, MIS on general graphs. This implies an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ worst-case barrier, not an $\Omega(\log n)$ barrier.

Their separate degree-reduction paper obtains $O(\log\Delta/\log(\log^{*}\Delta)+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds for girth at least seven. Its Open Question 1 asks for the general-graph improvement.

context_blocks.text: A sequential greedy algorithm can scan vertices and select each vertex whose neighbors have not been selected. The difficulty here is distributing those decisions: a processor sits at each vertex and initially sees only local information. After r communication rounds, it cannot have learned anything beyond distance r. Message size and local computation are free in LOCAL, so a lower bound measures the reach of coordination itself.

Maximal means that no further vertex can be added. It does not require the largest possible independent set. For example, on a star, either the center alone or all leaves is a valid answer. The challenge is to choose consistently across a general network, rather than to optimize the number of selected vertices.

Degree-sensitive algorithms achieve $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds. This is already sublogarithmic when the degree is sufficiently small; the unresolved target includes polynomial-degree graphs. Repeatedly making only constant-factor progress leaves a logarithmic running time.

Recent work breaks that pattern on graphs with no cycles of length at most six. It does not extend to arbitrary graphs. Together with stronger lower bounds, this leaves a concrete question: can local choices still make sufficiently rapid progress when short cycles create dependencies between nearby decisions?

cards.title: One-cycle versus two-cycles conjecture
cards.formal: For every fixed $0<\delta<1$, must every randomized MPC algorithm distinguishing one n-cycle from two vertex-disjoint \((n/2)\)-cycles use $\Omega(\log n)$ rounds in the worst case over even n and input placement? Each machine has $O(n^\delta)$ words and total memory is \(O(n)\) words. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each requested fixed $c>0$. An $o(\log n)$-round algorithm for one fixed $\delta<1$ would refute this lower-bound conjecture.
cards.why: I include this because the input removes most graph-theoretic complications and leaves the cost of assembling global connectivity information. It is a standard conditional-hardness benchmark for massively parallel algorithms, and a resolution would clarify whether limited memory creates an inherent logarithmic coordination cost even on degree-two graphs.
cards.definitions: Words have $O(\log n)$ bits. The input edge list is distributed across machines without exceeding their local memory. Each synchronous round allows arbitrary local computation followed by sending and receiving at most $O(n^{\delta})$ words per machine. The desired success probability is $1-n^{-c}$ for fixed $c>0$. This card fixes linear total memory; variants allowing more total space must be stated separately.

progress.text: Nanongkai and Scquizzato develop equivalence classes and conditional-hardness connections around this cycle problem and logarithmic-space computation. Their reductions have explicit global-memory requirements; those should be checked before transferring them to the linear-total-memory variant here.

Gan, Wirth, and Zhang explicitly state the linear-total-memory 2-CYCLE conjecture while giving a constant-round algorithm for embedded grid graphs. The promised arbitrary-cycle problem is left unresolved.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The lower bound is conjectural. Constant-round results for geometric graphs or larger local memory do not establish this variant.

context_blocks.text: Both promised inputs have exactly n vertices and n edges, and every vertex has degree two. Counting vertices, counting edges, and checking degrees therefore gives the same answer. The difference is how those edges join into components. Vertex identifiers are arbitrary, so the labels do not reveal where a cycle begins or whether two pieces belong together.

A sequential scan with graph traversal solves the problem in linear time. With the edge list spread across machines, no one machine can store the whole instance. Repeatedly joining path fragments or doubling the length represented by a pointer gives a natural logarithmic-round approach. The conjecture says that general distributed computation cannot compress this process into asymptotically fewer communication rounds under the stated memory limits.

It is tempting to justify the conjecture by saying that information travels only one graph edge per round. That would be incorrect here. Any machine may send to any other machine, and local computation between exchanges is unrestricted. The restriction is how much information a machine can store, send, and receive at once. A valid lower bound must cope with arbitrary encodings and nonlocal communication.

Extra geometric structure can change the answer. The 2025 grid-connectivity algorithm uses an embedding with bounded edge lengths to obtain constant rounds in its parameter regime. An arbitrarily labelled cycle does not provide that embedding, so the geometric result does not refute this promise-problem conjecture.

cards.title: Deterministic LOCAL MIS in \(O(\log  n)\) rounds
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that outputs a maximal independent set on every $n$-vertex simple graph in $O(\log n)$ synchronous communication rounds? Each vertex has a distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifier, and the guarantee must hold for every valid identifier assignment and every maximum degree. The output must be independent, and every vertex outside it must have a neighbor inside it. No random bits are available.
cards.why: This measures the quantitative cost of removing randomness from a basic distributed task. I include it separately from randomized sublogarithmic MIS because the algorithm must work against every identifier assignment with no failure probability. An \(O(\log  n)\) result would match the familiar randomized worst-case benchmark and propagate through reductions to other symmetry-breaking problems.
cards.definitions:
LOCAL allows unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. A vertex’s r-round view contains only its radius-r neighborhood and the identifiers and input data revealed there. The complexity is elapsed communication rounds until all vertices output. The target is uniform over arbitrary graphs, not restricted to bounded degree, planar graphs, or trees.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree; the time guarantee must still be \(O(\log  n)\) uniformly over degrees.

progress.text: Balliu and coauthors prove a deterministic lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\Delta,\log n/\log\log n\})$. In particular, the general worst-case complexity cannot be substantially below logarithmic up to a log-log factor.
Rozhoň and Ghaffari obtain polylogarithmic deterministic network decomposition and consequently polylogarithmic deterministic MIS.
Ghaffari and Grunau improve MIS to $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ rounds, where the hidden factors are polylogarithmic in $\log n$.
Bourreau, Brandt, and Nolin use the same deterministic MIS benchmark to improve \(\Delta\)-coloring; their result does not give an \(O(\log  n) \mathrm{MIS}\) algorithm.

context_blocks.text: Identifiers make deterministic symmetry breaking possible, but they do not automatically make it fast. Consider the rule that selects every vertex whose identifier is smaller than those of all its remaining neighbors, then removes the selected vertices and their neighbors. On a path with identifiers increasing from one endpoint to the other, each phase selects just the smallest remaining endpoint. This rule takes linearly many phases, even though much faster algorithms exist for paths.

Randomized MIS algorithms avoid adversarial identifier patterns by making new random choices. A deterministic algorithm has to arrange useful progress from the graph and identifiers alone. The existence of a good assignment of random choices is insufficient: processors must find suitable choices while paying for the communication that coordinates them.

Network decomposition supplied a general way to organize that work into small-diameter clusters that can be processed in groups. It settled the old question of whether polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is possible. The present target concerns the finer exponent and cannot be recorded as the already-solved polylogarithmic-time question.

Identifiers make deterministic symmetry breaking possible, but they do not automatically make it fast. Consider the rule that selects every vertex whose identifier is smaller than those of all its remaining neighbors, then removes the selected vertices and their neighbors. On a path with identifiers increasing from one endpoint to the other, each phase selects just the smallest remaining endpoint. cards.title: Subquadratic metric TSP cost estimation below factor two
cards.formal:
Do there exist an absolute constant \(\delta\in(0,1)\) and a classical randomized distance-query algorithm that estimates the minimum traveling-salesperson tour cost of every \(n\)-point metric within a factor \(2-\delta\), using \(o(n^2)\) distance queries?

For a metric \(d\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge3\), define
\[\operatorname{TSP}(d)=\min_{\pi\in\mathfrak S_n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}d\bigl(\pi(j),\pi(j+1)\bigr),\qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).\]
The algorithm knows \(n\) and can request \(d(i,j)\) for any chosen pair of labels. Its output \(Z\) must satisfy
\[\Pr\!\left[\operatorname{TSP}(d)\le Z\le(2-\delta)\operatorname{TSP}(d)\right]\ge\frac23\]
for every input metric. Only the number of oracle calls is bounded; the output is a cost estimate and need not describe a tour.
cards.why: This is a central test of how well a global optimization value can be estimated from incomplete metric information. Resolving it would determine whether the factor-two barrier is inherent to sparse distance access or reflects limitations of current estimators, with a sharp separation between learning a value and constructing a tour.

The question asks whether some fixed approximation factor below two is achievable with a subquadratic number of queries on every metric.

cards.definitions:
The input consists of a known integer \(n\ge3\), the labels \([n]\), and an oracle for a function \(d:[n]\times[n]\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). It is promised that \(d(i,j)=0\) exactly when \(i=j\), that \(d(i,j)=d(j,i)\), and that
\[d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\quad\text{for all }i,j,k\in[n].\]
Thus all off-diagonal distances are finite positive real numbers. The triangle inequality and symmetry are input promises, not properties that the algorithm must verify. Metrics are arbitrary: no Euclidean embedding, dimension bound, integer-distance restriction, bounded aspect ratio or distribution on inputs is supplied.

One query consists of specifying labels \(i,j\in[n]\) and receiving the exact real distance \(d(i,j)\). It costs one oracle call. Queries may depend on earlier replies and on the algorithm’s private randomness. Repeated calls are charged again. Diagonal values are known to be zero; allowing a paid diagonal call gives no additional information. The metric remains fixed throughout the execution and is chosen independently of the random bits.

The algorithm is uniform: a single finite program works for every \(n\). To specify computation with exact real oracle replies, use a classical real-register machine with rational program constants, ordinary finite control, integer counters, and exact real arithmetic and comparisons. Allowed real operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by a nonzero value; registers may store queried distances and calculated real values. Randomness consists of independent fair bits, which may be used to select labels. Integer computation, local arithmetic, storage and random-bit generation are not charged to the query budget. They must define an algorithm that halts with probability one on each input. No advice depending on the metric or on \(n\), quantum queries, further metric oracle, precomputed spanning tree or access to unqueried matrix entries is available.

This is a query-complexity question, so there is no polynomial-time or subquadratic-time requirement on the computation between calls. In particular, the original source’s suggestion of subquadratic total time is a stronger aspiration, not an additional condition for answering its primary query question. A positive solution with such a time bound would also solve this card, provided it meets all the stated guarantees.

The output \(Z\) is one real value. On a successful execution it is an upper estimate at most \(2-\delta\) times the optimum. An equivalent lower-estimate convention would require \(\operatorname{TSP}(d)/(2-\delta)\le Z'\le\operatorname{TSP}(d)\); multiplication by the fixed approximation factor converts between the conventions without oracle calls. The algorithm may fail to meet the interval on at most one third of its random executions. Success is required for each metric individually, not merely on average over an input distribution.

The query bound is worst case over inputs and random executions, apart from null-probability exceptional executions. Formally, there must exist \(q:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that every \(n\)-point input uses at most \(q(n)\) oracle calls with probability one, and
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{q(n)}{n^2}=0.\]
The constant \(\delta\), the program and this bound are independent of all distance values. There is no hidden dependence on the ratio of the largest to the smallest positive distance. For finitely many small \(n\), all pair distances may be queried without affecting the limit. The little-o condition is weaker than demanding \(O(n^{2-\gamma})\) for some fixed \(\gamma>0\); both a fixed polynomial saving and a genuine slower asymptotic saving would qualify.

The quantifier order is \(\exists\delta\;\exists A\;\exists q\;\forall n\ge3\;\forall d\), followed by probability over the execution of \(A\). The improvement \(\delta\) must be a positive constant; an approximation factor approaching two from below as \(n\) grows is insufficient. The card asks whether any such constant improvement exists, not for the largest possible improvement or a full approximation-query tradeoff.

A tour is a cyclic ordering of all labels, using each exactly once before returning to the start. The cost includes that closing edge. The oracle describes the complete metric, so each tour edge costs the queried distance itself; no separate underlying graph path needs to be output. \(\mathfrak S_n\) is the set of all permutations of \([n]\). The finite minimum in the definition of \(\operatorname{TSP}(d)\) is attained and is strictly positive.

For background, a spanning tree is a connected acyclic graph on all labels, and \(\operatorname{MST}(d)\) is the minimum sum of its edge distances. The familiar inequalities \(\operatorname{MST}(d)\le\operatorname{TSP}(d)\le2\operatorname{MST}(d)\) explain the factor-two threshold. Estimating the weight of an MST does not give its edges. A graphic metric is the shortest-path distance metric of a connected unweighted undirected graph. A \((1,2)\)-metric has every off-diagonal distance equal to one or two. Both are special classes of the general metric inputs here.

This is not a streaming task: a stream reveals entries in an imposed order, whereas the algorithm here chooses each pair it queries. A result that is given a minimum spanning tree as additional input, or promises a spanning tree of unit-distance edges, concerns additional information or structure absent from the target. Full-input approximation algorithms may also use quadratically many distance entries, regardless of their approximation ratio.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of an absolute \(\delta>0\), a uniform classical randomized algorithm and a worst-case query bound \(q(n)=o(n^2)\) with the stated success probability for every metric. A positive answer must prove the cost guarantee, the uniform little-o bound independent of the metric’s scale and aspect ratio, and almost-sure halting in the specified oracle model. It need not output a tour or run in subquadratic total time. A negative answer must refute this quantified existence statement for randomized adaptive algorithms; a lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, near-exact approximation, or a specific algorithm is insufficient. Positive results restricted to graphic or \((1,2)\)-metrics, or assuming an MST is supplied, do not resolve the arbitrary-metric target. Experimental success rates, conditional computational hardness and an improvement that vanishes with \(n\) do not establish the required result.

Classical tour algorithms can rely on an actual spanning tree and further global structure. The source emphasizes that obtaining the tree itself can require quadratically many distance queries even though estimating its total weight is much easier. This is an information-access distinction between value estimation and producing a witness.

Chen, Kannan and Khanna obtain below-two estimation for graphic and two-valued metrics. They also prove that sufficiently accurate approximation already requires quadratic query complexity on these special classes. That obstruction near factor one does not rule out every fixed improvement below two.

Chen, Khanna and Tan extend below-two estimation to positive integral metrics that either have a promised unit-edge spanning tree or are supplied with an MST. The query cost is \(\widetilde O(n^{3/2})\). Their paper explicitly leaves the unrestricted general-metric query question open.

The 2023 paper also gives streaming algorithms and lower bounds. Those theorems have different access rules and cannot be substituted for a pair-distance query theorem. In particular, a result with an extra pass over every matrix entry need not inspect only a subquadratic number of distances.

The requested estimate need not correspond to a tour produced by the algorithm. A positive answer would establish that useful information about tour cost is accessible with strictly fewer than all pairwise measurements, even where recovering the usual intermediate structures is expensive.

cards.definitions: For each integer \(N\geq2\), let \(f_N\) map every nonempty sequence over \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) of length at most \(N\) to one bit. Totality means every such sequence is in its domain. Order invariance means permuting any sequence leaves its value unchanged; it is stronger than merely swapping two players. A streaming algorithm is one fixed deterministic program given \(N\) in binary, which starts with an initialized state, reads one item at a time, and produces \(f_N(x)\) when the stream ends. There must be constants \(B,c\), depending on the family but not \(N\), for which initialization, each update and final output take at most \(B\log^c(N+2)\) steps, and the stored state and temporary workspace use that many bits. A merge scheme consists of three fixed deterministic programs: a map \(\Phi_N\) from one item to a summary, a map \(\mu_N\) from two summaries to a summary, and a decoder \(\eta_N\) from a summary to a bit. Summaries may include their represented length. For every valid sequence and every rooted binary tree whose leaves are its items in any order, apply \(\Phi_N\) at the leaves, \(\mu_N\) at internal nodes and \(\eta_N\) at the root. The resulting bit must equal \(f_N(x)\). Intermediate summaries may depend on the tree; only the decoded answer must be invariant. Each message, workspace and invocation time is bounded by \(B_1\log^{c_1}(N+2)\), for constants depending on the family. Time means steps of a standard deterministic multitape Turing machine on binary representations; input and output tapes have the usual sequential access. The programs receive \(N\) and their local arguments, with no advice or precomputed data depending on \(N\). Both models are exact and deterministic. The conclusion is existence of a merge scheme for each streaming-computable family, not a promised efficient compiler from arbitrary program descriptions.

Alternatively give a total symmetric family with a qualifying streaming algorithm and prove that no qualifying merge scheme exists. cards.title: Common2 membership of FIFO queues
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true?
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge3\quad
\exists A_n:\quad A_n\text{ implements a linearizable wait-free FIFO queue for }n\text{ processes}
\]
using only the atomic read/write registers and one-shot test-and-set bits defined below? The queue is initially empty and has no capacity bound. Every process may perform arbitrarily many operations of either kind, with arbitrary finite binary strings as enqueued values. Each \(A_n\) is deterministic and has finite code; it may depend on \(n\). The quantifiers do not additionally require one compiler producing all \(A_n\).
cards.definitions:
Fix \(n\ge3\). There are \(n\) named sequential processes with identifiers \(1,\ldots,n\), each knowing \(n\) and its own identifier. A process has unbounded private storage, initially containing only its identifier, \(n\), and its fixed program data. Its local computation is given by a deterministic finite Turing program on finite strings. Shared communication is confined to two countable arrays with natural-number addresses: registers \(R_0,R_1,\ldots\), initially containing the empty binary string, and bits \(B_0,B_1,\ldots\), initially zero. A register read atomically returns its whole current finite string; a write atomically replaces that string and returns an acknowledgement. The primitive \(\operatorname{TAS}(j)\) atomically returns the old value of \(B_j\) and changes it to one. A bit is never reset, and every later test-and-set on that bit returns one. Any process can access any address; using a previously unused address does not require an allocation oracle. There is no fixed bound on addresses used, register bit lengths, private storage or total operations over a whole execution. A finite execution prefix uses only finite data and finitely many primitive calls.

The scheduler interleaves individual local computation steps and atomic primitive calls. Each scheduled process chooses its next action from its private state, its current invocation and previous primitive responses. Processes receive no randomness, clock, failure detector, schedule information or noncomputable oracle. They can be delayed arbitrarily and can stop forever at any point. No fairness assumption constrains other processes. Local Turing steps, primitive invocations and operation responses count as that process's own steps; no bounded step complexity is demanded.

The sequential queue state is a finite sequence of finite binary strings, initially empty. \(\operatorname{Enqueue}(v)\) appends one occurrence of \(v\) at the end and returns a distinguished acknowledgement. \(\operatorname{Dequeue}()\) removes and returns the first occurrence if the sequence is nonempty; otherwise it returns a distinguished \(\mathsf{Empty}\) value without changing the state. Empty, acknowledgement and string-valued responses have separate tags, so the empty binary string is an ordinary possible item. Repeated equal values represent separate occurrences. Each process can invoke either operation whenever its previous invocation has returned, so it has at most one pending invocation. Clients may choose later invocations from earlier responses; there are no designated enqueuer or dequeuer roles, no bound on the number of calls and no promise that a dequeue finds an item.

Linearizability is required for every finite execution prefix. Take its history of queue invocations and responses. Append responses to any chosen subset of pending invocations and discard the other pending invocations. There must be a total order of the resulting completed operations that preserves each process's order, respects every real-time precedence in the completed history, and gives exactly their responses under the sequential queue specification. Here real-time precedence means that one operation's response occurs before the other's invocation. The choice of this total order may differ between different execution prefixes; it is not required to preserve earlier choices when a history is extended. Infinite executions must satisfy this safety condition at every finite prefix.

Wait-freedom is the following per-process termination property: from any reachable configuration with a pending operation of process \(p\), every continuation in which \(p\) takes infinitely many of its own steps contains a response to that operation after finitely many such steps, regardless of all other processes' delays, crashes or continuing operations. Thus an infinite execution in which one process's pending operation never finishes despite that process continuing to take steps is forbidden, even if other operations keep completing. These definitions specify ordinary linearizability and wait-freedom, with unlimited resource capacity; they impose neither strong linearizability nor a resource bound uniform over all histories.
cards.why: A queue orders work shared by concurrent processes. This question asks whether very weak synchronization suffices to guarantee that each continuing process finishes, even while others stop or interfere. It tests the distinction between consensus power and the ability to implement a reusable data type.

cards.title: Deterministic volume gap
cards.formal: For every locally checkable labeling problem \(\Pi\) on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree \(\Delta\), does the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm A with \(V_{A}(n)=o(n)\) imply the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm B with \(V_{B}(n)=O(1+\log * n)\)? Algorithms know the exact size of their input graph, and node identifiers are distinct integers in \(\{1,\ldots ,|V(G)|^{2}\}\). Here \(V_{A}(n)\) is the maximum number of distinct vertices visited to determine one vertex’s output, over all allowed instances with at most n vertices and all requested vertices.
cards.definitions: An LCL is specified by fixed \(\Delta \ge 2, a\) fixed verification radius \(r\ge 1\), finite nonempty input/output alphabets, and a finite set of permitted rooted radius-r labeled neighborhoods. Rules may inspect degrees and local ports, but not n or IDs. Instances include every finite nonempty simple undirected graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\), possibly disconnected, every input labeling and every port numbering. A labeling is valid exactly when all neighborhoods satisfy the rules. A deterministic VOLUME computation for a requested vertex v starts with v’s ID, degree, input, ports, \(\Pi\) and the exact |\(V(G)|\), and visited set \(\{v\}\). It may adaptively choose a visited vertex w and one of its incident ports, learning the neighbor u, its ID, degree, input and incident port names, then add u to the visited set. Arbitrary jumps to unseen IDs are forbidden. Only the number of distinct visited vertices, including v, is charged; local computation must terminate but its time and temporary space are unrestricted. Queries at different vertices run independently with no preprocessing or shared mutable state. Their outputs must jointly form a valid labeling for every input and ID assignment. Each algorithm is one finite computable program for all graph sizes. \(\log * n\) is the number of iterated base-2 logarithms needed to reach at most 1; the added 1 handles small n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication, or specify one fixed LCL with a sublinear-volume deterministic algorithm and prove it has no \(O(\log * n)\)-volume deterministic algorithm. Precisely, the latter lower bound means that for every correct B, every \(C>0\) and every \(n_{0}\), some \(n\ge n_{0}\) satisfies \(V_{B}(n)>C(1+\log * n)\). This gap formulation fixes the asymptotic quantifiers without assuming an optimal algorithm or an arbitrary symbolic complexity function exists.
cards.why: This tests whether deterministic access to local solutions has only a tiny-information regime and an essentially global regime. Either outcome would substantially constrain the design and possible complexity classes of deterministic local computation algorithms.

importance.reason: A proposed collapse of an entire deterministic complexity interval, rather than a bound for one task. It clarifies the power of adaptive exploration and the role of randomness in local computation.

progress.text: Rosenbaum and Suomela introduce the distance-versus-volume framework and pose the deterministic intermediate-volume question as Question 7.1. Their examples establish several randomized intermediate scales while retaining linear deterministic volume.

Brandt, Grunau, and Rozhoň show that randomized local computation below \(o(\sqrt{\log  n})\) can be sped up to deterministic \(O(\log * n)\). Their results also give linear deterministic volume lower bounds for fixed-color tree-coloring tasks in the relevant bounded-degree setting. These do not cover every LCL.
Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt close the gap between constant and iterated-logarithmic VOLUME complexity. The much larger interval above \(\log * n\) remains the issue here.
Suomela’s updated problem list retains the question of deterministic volume strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear.

Peng gives randomized VOLUME and LCA constructions of complexity \(\Theta (\log ^{k} n)\) for positive integers k and polynomial scales up to logarithmic factors. Section 1.1 explicitly leaves the deterministic gap unresolved.

context_blocks.text: A processor that sees far through a narrow part of a graph can inspect much less information than one that explores an entire ball of the same radius. The VOLUME model measures that inspected information. Its adaptive exploration captures a central feature of answering a query about a huge graph without first constructing an entire solution.

Correctness still couples the answers. Independently determining the color or matching status of one vertex must agree with the answers obtained for every other vertex. The algorithm cannot save previous answers and use their accumulated state as a growing global solution. This makes a low-volume construction substantially stronger than an arbitrary sequential greedy algorithm.

Rosenbaum and Suomela ask whether there is any deterministic volume complexity strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear, and conjecture there is none. Their model supplies exact graph size and polynomially bounded identifiers. Removing these conventions changes the indistinguishability arguments, so the card keeps them explicit.

The known small-complexity gaps leave the central interval unresolved. Randomized examples inhabit many intermediate scales, but an algorithm that follows a favorable random exploration does not automatically give a deterministic procedure that succeeds on every labeled graph. A deterministic counterexample to the proposed collapse would establish a new basic behavior.

July 2026 work constructs additional randomized polylogarithmic and polynomial volume complexities. Its introduction explicitly separates those results from the still-open deterministic question. The increased richness on the randomized side makes the contrast sharper while supplying no deterministic intermediate example.

cards.title: Factor-two graph distances in logarithmically many passes
cards.formal:
Can a randomized streaming algorithm estimate the distance between two specified vertices of an undirected, unweighted graph within a factor of two using \(O(\log n)\) passes and \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) bits of memory?

More precisely, do there exist one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), constants \(C_s,C_p>0\) and an integer \(k\ge0\) such that the following holds for every simple graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), every specified pair \(s,t\), and every ordering of its edges? The algorithm knows \(n,s,t\) before the stream begins, uses at most
\[C_s n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^k\text{ bits and }\left\lceil C_p\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil\text{ passes},\]
and, with probability at least \(2/3\), outputs \(D\) satisfying
\[d_G(s,t)\le D\le2d_G(s,t).\]
For disconnected \(s,t\), success means outputting the symbol \(\infty\). All passes read the same edge order.
cards.why: Shortest-path distance is a basic graph quantity whose global dependencies challenge small-memory sequential access. This question isolates the number of scans needed for a useful constant-factor estimate, between new near-logarithmic lower bounds and the best verified upper bounds.

Their constant-factor upper bound uses O((log n/log log n)^2) passes; their lower bound is Omega(log n/log log n), including fixed-pair unweighted instances and a same-order simulation. These statements leave the selected target unresolved. A bounded later-work search found no verified closure of this gap. No new algorithm, lower-bound proof or Lean formalization is claimed.

sentences: The problem asks for a factor-two estimate of one specified distance in an undirected unweighted graph stream.
The source and target are known in advance, and every pass sees the same arbitrary edge order.
The algorithm may use n times a fixed polylogarithmic number of bits but only logarithmically many passes.

cards.definitions:
The input graph is finite, undirected, unweighted and simple: there are no self-loops or parallel edges. Its vertices have distinct binary labels in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\). Each edge appears exactly once as an unordered pair of labels. The stream lists these edges explicitly in an arbitrary order, with an end marker; it may be empty. Isolated vertices are included in the known vertex set even though they do not appear in any edge. No planarity, sparsity, degree or diameter restriction is imposed.

The vertices \(s,t\) belong to the known vertex set and are supplied before any edge is read. They may be equal. A path has length equal to its number of edges, and \(d_G(s,t)\) is the minimum length of a path from \(s\) to \(t\). Set \(d_G(s,s)=0\) and \(d_G(s,t)=\infty\) if there is no connecting path. Every finite distance is an integer between zero and \(n-1\).

A pass scans the edge list once from beginning to end. After a pass the algorithm may rewind to the beginning and retain its memory, but it cannot reorder or change the stream. Within a pass it has only sequential access. There is no random access to old edges, adjacency-query oracle, external scratch file or separate stored copy of the graph. All passes encounter the same fixed order. The algorithm may stop after fewer passes than its bound; starting another scan counts as another pass.

The output is one integer \(D\) or the distinguished symbol \(\infty\). The algorithm need not output a path, a spanning tree, distances to other targets or a summary supporting later queries. Integer output loses no generality for this factor guarantee: rounding down a nonnegative real estimate in the permitted interval preserves both inequalities when the true distance is an integer. For a connected pair the successful output lies between \(d_G(s,t)\) and \(2d_G(s,t)\), with no additive error. For a disconnected pair the successful output is \(\infty\); for \(s=t\) it is zero.

For every fixed graph, edge ordering and pair, probability is over the algorithm's independent fair random bits. The input and its order are fixed independently of those bits. The success condition concerns the single requested output. It is not an average over graphs or stream orders, and it does not require one random seed to work for all inputs simultaneously.

Use one finite uniform program for every input size. Its memory consists of all mutable working information, including retained edge data, vertex labels, counters, stored random choices and output preparation. Every bit of that information counts. Fresh random bits may be read as needed, but old random bits cannot be revisited unless their information was retained within the space bound. The graph stream is read-only external input. The supplied parameters take only \(O(\log(n+2))\) bits, so charging their storage does not change the target.

Both resource bounds hold throughout every execution, including unsuccessful random executions. The algorithm must halt and produce an output; no bound on local computation time is imposed beyond this termination requirement. Thus the question isolates memory and passes, as in the streaming source. Computationally expensive processing between edges cannot hide extra memory or reread the input. A polynomial local-time algorithm would suffice, but such a time requirement is not added to the target.

The constants \(C_s,C_p\) and the exponent \(k\) are fixed independently of \(n\), the graph, the stream order, the distance and the random choices. The memory notation \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) permits any fixed power of the logarithm. The pass bound permits only one power: an arbitrary \(O(\log^c n)\) bound for a fixed \(c>1\) is not the requested \(O(\log n)\) result. Binary logarithms with the harmless \(n+2\) offset avoid small-input exceptions.

The term semi-streaming refers to memory proportional to the number of vertices times a fixed power of the logarithm, even though a dense graph can have quadratically many edges. Papers often count \(O(\log n)\)-bit words rather than bits. This changes the permitted logarithmic power by one and therefore describes the same space class here. When a particular logarithmic space bound is quoted, its unit must still be stated.

The selected model is insertion-only and allows every fixed edge ordering. Edge deletions, random-order streams and a source or target revealed only after streaming are separately quantified variants. Likewise, all-pairs distances and single-source shortest-path trees ask for more output than this card. The original source combines several of these questions. With the user's approval, this card retains just factor-two estimation of one known pair in logarithmically many passes.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the algorithm and constants in the statement, including its success probability for every graph and order and its worst-case bit-space and pass bounds. Alternatively, provide a complete Lean-checked proof that no such uniform randomized algorithm exists. The negative direction must rule out every fixed polylogarithmic space exponent \(k\) together with an \(O(\log n)\) pass bound; a lower bound for one narrower space allowance does not suffice. context_blocks.text: A graph may contain far more edges than a small-memory algorithm can retain. One scan can reveal useful local connections, while a short path between distant vertices can depend on edges encountered in an inconvenient order. The question asks how much repeated access is needed even when only one numerical distance is requested.

Such a summary supports many pairs, whereas this card supplies its only pair in advance. Results that exploit all-pairs summaries do not by themselves characterize the best method for that smaller output requirement.

Exact distance can be obtained with a number of passes depending on the distance. That dependence can be large on arbitrary graphs. The selected target instead demands a logarithmic worst-case pass bound and permits a controlled multiplicative error.

cards.title: Linear-sketch complexity of the nuclear norm
cards.formal:
Determine the optimal number \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) of exact real linear measurements required to estimate the nuclear norm of an arbitrary real \(n\times n\) matrix with relative error at most \(\varepsilon\) and success probability at least \(2/3\), up to matching constant factors in \(n\), for every fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\).

The sketch is randomized and chosen independently of the input matrix. It must satisfy, for every fixed \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\),
\[\Pr_\omega\!\left[(1-\varepsilon)\|A\|_*\le d_\omega(S_\omega A)\le(1+\varepsilon)\|A\|_*\right]\ge\frac23,\]
where \(S_\omega:\mathbb R^{n\times n}\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(d_\omega\) is a decoder that receives only the sketch and the input-independent random choices. The quantity \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) is the smallest possible dimension \(m\).

Give an explicit asymptotic description \(g(n,\varepsilon)\) and prove that for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) there exist \(0<c_\varepsilon\le C_\varepsilon<\infty\) and \(N_\varepsilon\) such that
\[c_\varepsilon g(n,\varepsilon)\le m_\varepsilon(n)\le C_\varepsilon g(n,\varepsilon)\qquad(n\ge N_\varepsilon).\]
The constants may depend on the fixed accuracy, but not on \(n\). Logarithmic factors in \(n\) must be resolved; determining only a polynomial exponent does not meet this target.
cards.why: Determining this complexity would explain whether summing singular values permits a materially smaller linear summary than storing a general matrix, and exactly how much compression is possible. It would also locate a central matrix norm within the sharply differing sketching behavior of the Schatten family.
cards.status_note: The exact asymptotic order up to constant factors remains source-open in the checked material. The original question is Woodruff’s 2014 survey Open Question 4. The 2019 journal article’s model and linear lower bound were checked. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 found Yang’s arXiv:2608.22247v3, revised 27 August 2026: its stated near-quadratic lower and upper bounds leave logarithmic factors unresolved, as explicitly discussed in §6. This review inspected its model, theorem statement and remaining-gap discussion, not a full independent verification of its 94-page proof; no verified journal acceptance is asserted. The recent bounds are therefore identified as preprint claims, and even as stated they do not complete this card’s matching-constant-factor criterion.

sentences: The nuclear norm of a matrix is the sum of its singular values.
The question asks for the smallest number of randomized exact real linear measurements that suffice to approximate this norm for every fixed input matrix.
The requested answer must give matching upper and lower bounds up to constant factors for each fixed relative accuracy.

cards.definitions:
Let \(n\) be any positive integer. For a real square matrix \(A\), its singular values \(\sigma_1(A),\ldots,\sigma_n(A)\) are the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of \(A^{\mathsf T}A\), with multiplicities and zeros included. Its nuclear norm, also called the trace norm or Schatten-1 norm, is
\[\|A\|_*=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_i(A).\]
No symmetry, positive-semidefiniteness, rank, sparsity, integrality or bounded-entry promise is imposed. In particular, this is not the entrywise sum of absolute values. A symmetric positive semidefinite matrix has nonnegative eigenvalues, and for that restricted class the nuclear norm equals the trace; the target covers all real matrices.

An \(m\)-measurement randomized linear sketch for given \(n,\varepsilon\) is specified by an input-independent probability space of random seeds \(\omega\), a real linear map \(S_\omega\), and a decoding function \(d_\omega:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\). Equivalently, each measurement has the form
\[(S_\omega A)_t=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n B_{tij}(\omega)A_{ij},\qquad1\le t\le m,\]
where all coefficients are fixed once the seed is sampled, before inspecting any entry of \(A\). The map may depend on \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(A\). The seed may also specify independent decoder randomness. The coefficient functions and the combined decoding map \((\omega,y)\mapsto d_\omega(y)\) are measurable with respect to their probability space and the usual Borel sigma-algebra on finite-dimensional real spaces, so every displayed success probability is defined.

All randomness is over the seed. The matrix is fixed before that seed is chosen, with the quantifier order \(\exists\text{ sketch distribution}\;\forall A\;\Pr_\omega[\text{success on }A]\ge2/3\). The same seed need not work simultaneously for all matrices. Conversely, a guarantee only for a random input matrix is insufficient. For \(A=0\), success requires the output to be exactly zero. For nonzero inputs the error bound is multiplicative, equivalently \(|d_\omega(S_\omega A)-\|A\|_*|\le\varepsilon\|A\|_*\).

The cost is the fixed number \(m\) of data-dependent real scalars retained. Coefficients, measurements and arithmetic are exact real objects. Their bit lengths, the description of the seed, evaluation time, and the decoder's auxiliary working space are not counted. No finite-precision or efficient-sampling requirement is added. The decoder can be nonlinear and have unbounded computational cost. This is an information measure for general linear sketches, not a claim of a Turing-machine implementation. Separate choices of distribution and decoder for each \(n,\varepsilon\) are allowed; an algorithm constructing them uniformly in polynomial time is not part of the target.

Define
\[m_\varepsilon(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\text{ an admissible }m\text{-measurement sketch satisfies the stated guarantee}\}.\]
This minimum is finite and attained as a minimum over integers: retaining all \(n^2\) entries is a linear sketch from which the norm is defined exactly. The target seeks a noncircular asymptotic description of this optimization, with upper bounds witnessed by admissible sketch distributions and lower bounds applying to every such distribution and decoder.

A restricted bilinear sketch retains a matrix \(UAV\) for input-independent matrices \(U\) and \(V\); its scalar entry count is one possible general linear-sketch dimension. General sketches are not restricted to this form. Lower bounds for one selected architecture do not automatically extend to all real linear maps. Likewise, bits of streaming memory and real measurement dimension are different resources. An entry update can be reflected linearly in the sketch, but this does not identify the number of exact counters with their finite binary storage cost.

The source asks for a constant-factor approximation without fixing the constant. This review spells out the family of fixed relative accuracies \(0<\varepsilon<1\), with constant success probability \(2/3\), in the standard model made explicit in the subsequent literature. Each accuracy is held constant while \(n\to\infty\); the answer need not optimize a joint regime where \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero with \(n\). The requested precision for the optimal dimension is equality of asymptotic order up to multiplicative constants, including every unbounded logarithmic factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular asymptotic description of \(m_\varepsilon(n)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching upper and lower bounds for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), with the quantifiers and input domain above. An upper bound must give a valid input-independent sketch and decoder with the per-matrix success guarantee. A lower bound must apply to arbitrary measurable decoders and all general randomized real linear maps. Bounds matching only up to polylogarithmic factors, only the exponent in \(n^{\alpha+o(1)}\), a result confined to positive semidefinite matrices, or a finite-bit streaming bound alone do not determine the requested order. The parameter \(\varepsilon\) is the sketch's relative error; the benchmark's default additive numerical tolerance does not replace the required asymptotic precision.

source_formulation.text: Woodruff asks for the optimal dimension of a linear sketch that approximates the Schatten-1, or nuclear, norm within a constant factor. The question contrasts it with the much better understood Frobenius and spectral norms.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Open Question 4, with the general real linear-sketch model and constant-factor precision made explicit below

context_blocks.text: The nuclear norm sums the strengths of all singular directions of a matrix. It is a standard matrix norm with uses in low-rank modeling, and its sketching complexity asks how much linear information must be retained to estimate that total without retaining the full matrix.

The neighboring Schatten norms behave very differently: for fixed approximation accuracy, the Frobenius norm admits a constant-dimensional sketch, whereas spectral-norm approximation requires \(\Theta(n^2)\) dimensions. The nuclear norm has long occupied an unresolved position between these extremes.

For real matrices, changing an entry changes the singular values indirectly. Ordinary vector norm sketches therefore do not automatically estimate a Schatten norm. The 2019 paper makes this distinction and connects nuclear-norm sketching to the possibility of small summaries for matrix nearest-neighbor search.

Theorem 4.1 of the 2019 paper gives an \(\Omega(n)\) general-sketch lower bound for nuclear-norm approximation at a sufficiently small fixed relative error. Its stated error probability can be converted to the convention here by constant repetition. The theorem does not by itself identify the optimum or assert the same threshold for every coarse approximation factor.

The August 2026 preprint claims, for each fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), constants \(A_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon\) with
\[\frac{n^2}{(\log n)^{A_\varepsilon}}\le m_\varepsilon(n)\le C_\varepsilon\frac{n^2\{\log\log(e^e n)\}^2}{\log(en)}\]
for sufficiently large \(n\). These are the claims of its Theorem 1.1, whose full proof has not been independently verified in this review. The paper explicitly retains a logarithmic gap, so the displayed bounds would still fall short of the card’s constant-factor target.

The short description of a “sketch” can hide several inequivalent costs. This card fixes the number of exact real measurements and a guarantee for each fixed matrix. Finite-bit streaming, input-dependent measurements, and recovery of the matrix itself have different requirements.

cards.title: One-pass semi-streaming depth-first search
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform randomized one-pass streaming algorithm and fixed constants \(C\ge1\), \(k\ge0\) that, for every connected simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) vertices, outputs a depth-first-search spanning tree using at most
\[C n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^k\]
bits of working memory, with probability at least \(2/3\) for every ordering of its edge stream?

The stream lists each edge once, contains no deletions, and can only be scanned from beginning to end. The algorithm may choose the root and neighbor order of the DFS tree. The question concerns the memory and pass bounds, with no additional polynomial-time requirement.

cards.definitions:
The graph has labelled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), is connected and undirected, and has no self-loops or parallel edges. The algorithm is given \(n\) in advance. Its input stream is an arbitrary permutation of the edges \(\{u,v\}\in E\), represented by the two binary vertex labels, followed by an end marker. No adjacency lists, neighbor-query oracle, random access to the graph or second scan are available. The empty stream for \(n=1\) is valid. The requirement is a promise on these well-formed connected graph streams; recognition of the promise is not an additional task.

A rooted spanning tree \(T\) consists of a root \(r\in V\) and one parent in \(V\) for each other vertex, with every parent edge belonging to \(E\). Following parents must reach \(r\) and visit no cycle. A vertex \(u\) is an ancestor of \(v\) when it lies on the tree path from \(r\) to \(v\). The required DFS condition is
\[\forall\{u,v\}\in E:\quad u\text{ is an ancestor of }v\ \text{or}\ v\text{ is an ancestor of }u.\]
For undirected graphs this characterizes a spanning tree obtainable by depth-first search: start at the root, recursively finish exploring a newly discovered neighbor before exploring another, and retain the edges used for first discovery. The root and each vertex's order of neighbors may be chosen by the algorithm. No prescribed or lexicographic traversal must be reproduced, and the neighbor order need not equal edge-arrival order. An arbitrary spanning tree need not satisfy the ancestor condition.

The output is an explicit root and parent table on all \(n\) labels; for \(n=1\), the sole vertex is the root. It has \(O(n\log(n+2))\) bits. The output may be produced after the stream ends using only retained memory and fresh randomness. A write-only output tape cannot be reread as extra storage. Deferring the output to the end does not change semi-streaming feasibility: an earlier root/parent output of this size could instead be retained within the same asymptotic memory regime.

The algorithm has a single finite description, independent of \(n\) and of the graph. It processes the input in one left-to-right pass and may keep at most \(C n(\log_2(n+2))^k\) bits at any time, including retained edges, summaries, counters, random seeds, temporary computation and postprocessing. The bound is worst case over valid streams and random choices. No advice or external writable storage is allowed. Fresh fair random bits are independent of the graph and edge order; old random bits can be accessed again only if retained within the memory bound. The algorithm must finish processing and produce an output with probability one, but no numerical bound on its processing time is imposed. In particular, the question does not silently add efficient offline computation to the streaming space restriction.

For every fixed \(G\) and every fixed edge permutation chosen before the random bits, the probability that the entire root/parent table is a valid DFS tree must be at least \(2/3\). An invalid tree or failure symbol counts as failure. Deterministic algorithms are allowed as a special case. This is a guarantee on arbitrary graphs and orders, not on random graphs or random-order streams.

Semi-streaming space here means \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) bits with one fixed exponent. A word of \(O(\log n)\) bits changes only that exponent, but arbitrary-precision words do not have unit storage cost. The source studies both insertion-only and insertion-deletion streams and states its lower-bound convention for insertion-only streams. This card retains the one-pass question in that basic insertion-only setting. A result only for streams with deletions would not refute it, while an algorithm handling deletions would be a stronger positive result.

A negative answer means that no pair of constants \(C,k\) and no such randomized algorithm works on every promised stream. It need not establish a full quadratic-space lower bound: any lower bound excluding \(n(\log n)^k\) for every fixed \(k\) would suffice. Extra passes, a restriction to sparse graphs with \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) edges, or a prescribed traversal order change the problem.

cards.definitions:
Graphs are finite, nonempty, simple and undirected; they may be disconnected and have arbitrary degree. A graph property \(P\) is a set of these graphs invariant under graph isomorphism. Vertices have no identifiers, port numbers, input labels, advice or knowledge of the graph order. Graph distance is the minimum number of edges in a path; vertices in different components have infinite distance.

Fix integers \(d\ge1\) and \(b\ge0\). A certificate assignment is any function \(z:V(G)\to\{0,1\}^{b}\); for \(b=0\) there is one empty certificate. At a root \(v\), the radius-\(d\) view consists of the root, all vertices at distance at most \(d\), their certificates, and precisely the graph edges with at least one endpoint at distance at most \(d-1\) from \(v\). Edges between two vertices at distance exactly \(d\) are not visible. Neither edges leading beyond the view nor the degrees of its boundary vertices outside the view are additional input.

A verifier is one finite deterministic Turing-machine program accepting or rejecting a view. A view is encoded by its finite adjacency matrix, root index and certificate strings; the decision must be invariant under all renumberings of that encoding. Thus encoding indices convey no persistent identifiers. The program halts on every finite view. Its running time and memory are unrestricted, and it may depend on \(P,d,b\), but it is the same program for every graph order and every vertex. It has no oracle, random bits or additional input.

Such a verifier certifies \(P\) with \(b\) bits when, for every allowed graph \(G\),
\[
G\in P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z:V(G)\to\{0,1\}^{b}\ \ \forall v\in V(G),\
A(\operatorname{view}_d(G,z,v))=\operatorname{accept}.
\]
The existential certificate assignment is unrestricted and may depend on the entire graph. On a graph outside \(P\), every assignment must cause at least one vertex to reject. There is no error probability. The cost is the common maximum number \(b\) of certificate bits stored at a vertex, not the total number of bits in the graph or view. Using a subset of the \(2^b\) strings is allowed.

Define \(c_d(P)\) as the least such integer \(b\), with value \(+\infty\) if no such verifier exists. The domain of the maximum in \(F(s,d)\) consists only of properties with a certificate bound \(s\) independent of graph order. Different properties and different values of \(d\) may use different verifiers; no algorithm receiving a description of \(P\) is required. The set of possible values is a nonempty subset of \(\{0,\ldots,s\}\): the property containing every graph has cost zero, and a radius-\(d\) verifier can restrict its input to radius one. Hence this maximum is finite and attained as a numerical value. All graphs, graph orders, properties and degrees in its definition are quantified; neither \(s\) nor \(d\) is hidden in an unspecified constant.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a mathematically specified function \(g:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that \(\lvert g(s,d)-F(s,d)\rvert\le1/100\) for every \(s\ge0,d\ge1\). The approximation need not be integer-valued. An unambiguous expression or certified rule can specify \(g\); merely repeating the defining maximum, giving sampled values, or proving only asymptotic upper or lower bounds does not determine this function to the required precision.

cards.title: Two-dimensional sandpile prediction in NC
cards.formal: Is the language \(\mathrm{SP}_2\) defined below in logspace-uniform \(\mathrm{NC}\)? An instance explicitly supplies a finite stable rectangular array of sand grains and cells \(p,q\) inside that rectangle. Extend the array by zero to all of \(\mathbb Z^2\), add one grain at \(p\), and accept exactly when \(q\) eventually topples under the simultaneous four-neighbor rule. The question concerns one uniform circuit family with polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth for all input lengths.
cards.definitions:
Let \(W,H\ge1\), let \(B=\{0,\ldots,W-1\}\times\{0,\ldots,H-1\}\), let \(c:B\to\{0,1,2,3\}\), and let \(p=(p_x,p_y),q=(q_x,q_y)\in B\). Define \(\bar c(v)=c(v)\) on \(B\) and \(\bar c(v)=0\) elsewhere in \(\mathbb Z^2\). Set \(c_0(v)=\bar c(v)+\mathbf1_{\{v=p\}}\). With
\[
E=\{(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)\},
\]
define, for every integer \(t\ge0\) and every \(v\in\mathbb Z^2\),
\[
c_{t+1}(v)=c_t(v)-4\mathbf1_{\{c_t(v)\ge4\}}+
\sum_{e\in E}\mathbf1_{\{c_t(v-e)\ge4\}}.
\]
Here \(\mathbf1_A\) is \(1\) when assertion \(A\) holds and \(0\) otherwise. Every unstable cell topples once per simultaneous round; its threshold and the number of grains sent to each neighbor are fixed. The required output is \(1\) exactly when \(\exists t\ge0:\ c_t(q)\ge4\). All cells outside the supplied rectangle participate in the same dynamics. There is no absorbing boundary, periodic identification, missing neighbor or cell-dependent weight.

For a nonnegative integer \(z\), let \(s(z)\) be its ordinary binary expansion without leading zeros, using \(s(0)=0\), and let \(b(z)=|s(z)|\). Encode \(z\) as \(1^{b(z)}0s(z)\). A valid binary input is the concatenation of these codes for \(W,H,p_x,p_y,q_x,q_y\), followed by exactly \(2WH\) bits encoding the entries of \(c\): list rows in increasing \(y\), and within each row increasing \(x\), using \(00,01,10,11\) for \(0,1,2,3\). Dimensions must be positive and the encoded coordinates must belong to \(B\). Strings not meeting these conditions are rejected. Let \(N\) be the complete binary string length, including all array entries. Extra zero rows or columns are permitted, but their entries still count; this is not a sparse or succinct configuration encoding.

Membership in logspace-uniform \(\mathrm{NC}\) means that there exist fixed integers \(a,k\ge1\), a fixed real \(K\ge1\), and a deterministic finite Turing-machine program generating a Boolean circuit \(C_N\) from the unary input \(1^N\), for every \(N\ge0\). It must halt, use at most \(K\log_2(N+2)\) work-tape cells, and write an explicit gate-and-wire description to a write-only output tape. Its input tape is read-only. The circuit has \(N\) input bits and one output, uses AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one and constants \(0,1\), has at most \(K(N+2)^a\) gates and depth at most \(K(\log_2(N+2))^k\), and decides \(\mathrm{SP}_2\) exactly on all length-\(N\) strings. Gate descriptions use binary indices in topological order and specify the output gate. There is no advice or oracle. The constants, circuit generator and gate basis are independent of the instance. Randomized error is not allowed; no time \(t\) is supplied as part of the instance.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of membership of this language in the specified uniform circuit class, or a complete Lean proof that no such circuit family and generator exist. Polynomial sequential simulation alone is insufficient. A proof of P-completeness under logspace reductions would imply nonmembership only with the additional assumption that P differs from NC; it is not an unconditional negative answer.

cards.definitions: The domain consists of all fixed total functions \(\phi\) with \(\phi(t,t)=0\) for every \(t\geq0\), whose rational value on binary integers \(a,b\) can be computed in time polynomial in \(\log(a+b+2)\). Numerators and positive denominators are output in binary; the polynomial may depend on \(\phi\). Symmetry, the triangle inequality, homogeneity and dependence only on \(a-b\) are not assumed. A stream starts with \(f=g=0\) in \(\mathbb N_0^n\). Each item selects one vector, a coordinate \(i\in[n]\), and a change \(+1\) or \(-1\); no intermediate coordinate may become negative. The total number of updates is at most a given bound \(M\geq1\), so all coordinates are at most \(M\). Inputs \(n,M\) and a rational accuracy \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) are known in advance. The algorithm reads each update once, in an arbitrary order independent of its coins, and at the end outputs a nonnegative rational \(D\). For every valid stream it must satisfy \((1-\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\) with probability at least \(2/3\); zero dissimilarity must therefore produce zero on a successful execution. The algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine that may depend on the fixed function \(\phi\). It may read fresh independent random bits, but remembered randomness, counters, work tapes and evaluation of \(\phi\) all count toward its working space. The read-once input and final write-only output are separate tapes and cannot serve as auxiliary storage. No running-time bound is required beyond termination on every run. Define \(\chi(\phi)=1\) if there are such an algorithm and constants \(B,a,b\), depending only on \(\phi\), using at most \(B\varepsilon^{-b}\log^a(n+M+2)\) working bits on every input and every coin outcome; otherwise define \(\chi(\phi)=0\). This definition ranges over all \(n,M,\varepsilon\). It does not require that a single decision program classify arbitrary descriptions of \(\phi\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a noncircular necessary-and-sufficient condition on the numerical function \(\phi\), expressed without quantifying over streaming algorithms or communication protocols, and prove the classification completely in Lean. The positive direction must establish the specified approximation scheme; the negative direction must rule out every space bound of the stated form. As a function-valued benchmark answer, a supplied real-valued classification \(h\) must satisfy \(|h(\phi)-\chi(\phi)|\leq1/100\) throughout the domain. An exact zero-one characterization satisfies this tolerance. Repeating the definition of \(\chi\), covering only a proper subclass, or giving an uncertified list of examples is insufficient.

Editorial specialization: this card fixes the separable, effectively evaluable rational-valued family, one-pass nonnegative-frequency deletion model and polylogarithmic-space approximation regime. The classification function makes the domain and acceptance precision explicit without requiring an algorithm to decide the classification from source code.

The source gives a linear-space obstruction when the cost of the same coordinate difference varies too much with its offset. This explains why dependence on the vector difference is a natural candidate property, but a necessary obstruction alone does not classify all admissible functions or provide matching algorithms.

The admissible family includes \(\phi(a,b)=|a-b|\), \(\phi(a,b)=(a-b)^2\), and coordinate disagreement \(\phi(a,b)=1\) when \(a\ne b\), zero otherwise. The last is not homogeneous. Thus “must be a norm” cannot be used literally as the characterization of every dissimilarity covered by the question.

Braverman, Chestnut, Woodruff and Yang characterize a large class of sums \(\sum_i h(|f_i-g_i|)\), including nonmonotone functions, with a specific exceptional class. Their work explicitly describes this as a partial answer to the Guha–Indyk question. It does not cover arbitrary two-argument \(\phi\).

The source’s norm-sketching update concerns a geometric characterization for normed spaces and a different constant-size communication formulation. Khot and Naor subsequently show that the corresponding norm characterization fails for general metric spaces. Neither statement is a characterization of the whole streaming class defined here.

An additive error proportional to the total frequency would be much weaker when two large vectors are very close. Relative error and exact treatment of zero are therefore central to the lower bounds and must be retained. Insertion-only algorithms or summaries of normalized probability distributions have different guarantees and input models.
